title: English Vocabulary 1 · Units 23–24
description: Units 23–24 checked against the illustrated teaching pages and exercises. Includes original example sentences, English usage guidance, and British English IPA.
sourceNotice: Vocabulary and usage targets were selected with reference to the user-supplied published reference material. Examples and explanatory notes are original; exercises and illustrations are not reproduced.

audit.scope: Reviewed Unit 23 illustrated sports, go/play/do patterns, locations, and exercises 23.1–23.4; Unit 24 film genres, people in films, cinema dialogues, common mistakes, and exercises 24.1–24.5. Existing learning-target IDs are preserved.
audit.pronunciation: British English phonemic forms checked against the textbook phonemic index on PDF pages 160–170 where indexed. Compound phrases reviewed compositionally, without independent dictionary verification of every utterance.
audit.cannotGuarantee: Static checks do not certify application import, text-to-speech quality, listening or pronunciation scoring, adaptive learning, progress restoration or backup/restore. A human editorial sign-off and browser-level checks remain outstanding.

editorialReview.reviewMethod: Inspected all four illustrated source pages and exercises 23.1–23.4 and 24.1–24.5; reviewed existing entries individually, checked applicable headwords against the book phonemic index, and performed static structural, provenance, stable-ID, and English-only checks.
editorialReview.notes: No original package, unit or vocabulary IDs were changed or removed. Browser-level importer, listening, pronunciation, speech synthesis and backup/restore were not tested.

units.title: Unit 23 — Sports
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 23. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: We play football after school.
items.note: In British English, football usually means association football (soccer). Say play football.

items.example: My uncle enjoys watching rugby.
items.note: Rugby is a ball game played by teams, usually on a pitch. Use play rugby.

items.example: They play American football on Sundays.
items.note: American football is different from football in standard British English. It is a ball game played by teams.

items.example: We play basketball in the sports centre.
items.note: A team ball game played on a court. Use play basketball.

items.example: I play badminton with my sister.
items.note: Players hit a shuttlecock over a net. Say play badminton, not do badminton.

items.example: They play baseball at the weekend.
items.note: A team ball game using a bat and ball. Say play baseball.

items.example: I like playing tennis on Saturdays.
items.note: Say play tennis, not go tennis or do tennis.

items.example: She plays volleyball for her school.
items.note: A team ball game in which players hit a ball over a net. Say play volleyball.

items.example: We play table tennis indoors.
items.note: A game played across a small table with bats and a light ball; also informally called ping-pong.

items.example: I play football every Friday.
items.note: Use play with football and other team ball games. The past tense is played.

items.example: Can you play tennis?
items.note: Use play tennis for this ball game; go tennis is incorrect.

items.example: They play basketball after lunch.
items.note: Use play with basketball and other ball games. The third-person form is plays basketball.

items.example: Running is good exercise.
items.note: The sport or activity of running. Use go running when talking about doing the activity.

items.example: My father enjoys sailing.
items.note: Travelling or competing in a boat powered by wind; the usual activity collocation is go sailing.

items.example: My brother watches motor racing.
items.note: Racing motor vehicles as a sport. You can watch motor racing; go motor racing refers to taking part.

items.example: Swimming is my favourite sport.
items.note: Moving through water as a sport or activity. Common collocation: go swimming.

items.example: We go kayaking on the lake.
items.note: Travelling or competing in a kayak. A kayak is a small narrow boat; use go kayaking.

items.example: She does judo twice a week.
items.note: A Japanese martial art. Say do judo, not go judo or play judo.

items.example: He does karate on Tuesdays.
items.note: A Japanese martial art. Say do karate, not play karate.

items.example: We went skiing in winter.
items.note: Travelling down snowy slopes on skis. Use go skiing; the past tense is went skiing.

items.example: She likes watching horse racing.
items.note: A sport in which horses race. Horse racing is often watched, and go horse racing can mean take part in racing or attend a race meeting depending on context.

items.example: Snowboarding looks exciting.
items.note: Travelling on snow on a single board. Use go snowboarding.

items.example: I go running before work.
items.note: Go + an -ing activity is a common pattern. Past tense: went running.

items.example: Do you go swimming at weekends?
items.note: Use go swimming rather than play swimming. It refers to doing the activity, not necessarily competing.

items.example: We go skiing every January.
items.note: The phrase is go skiing, with -ing. Past tense: went skiing.

items.example: They go kayaking in summer.
items.note: Use go + kayaking for the activity. Kayaking can take place on a lake, river or sea.

items.example: Let's go sailing tomorrow.
items.note: The go + -ing pattern is used for this outdoor activity. The past tense is went sailing.

items.example: My friend does judo.
items.note: Use do with martial arts such as judo. She does judo is third-person singular.

items.example: My cousin does karate.
items.note: Use do with this martial art. Do not say play karate.

items.example: There is a tennis court near my house.
items.note: Tennis is played on a tennis court; use the preposition on.

items.example: We booked a badminton court.
items.note: A court marked out for badminton. Say play badminton on a badminton court.

items.example: The volleyball court is outside.
items.note: A court for volleyball; use on for the playing surface.

items.example: The children are on the basketball court.
items.note: A court for basketball; say on a basketball court.

items.example: The teams are on the football pitch.
items.note: A field for football, called a football pitch in British English rather than a football court.

items.example: They are training on the rugby pitch.
items.note: A field for rugby. Use on a rugby pitch.

items.example: I go to the swimming pool every week.
items.note: A place designed for swimming. Use swim in a swimming pool, but go to the swimming pool.

items.example: Our town has a new sports centre.
items.note: British English spelling; American English sports center. A facility where several sports can be practised.

items.example: We play tennis on a court.
items.note: Use on with courts: on a tennis court, on a badminton court.

items.example: They play rugby on a pitch.
items.note: Use on with a football or rugby pitch, meaning the playing field.

items.example: Do you do any sports in your free time?
items.note: A general way to ask whether someone participates in sport. Here do means practise or take part in.

items.example: Do you play football at school?
items.note: Use play in questions about football and other ball games.

items.example: What's your favourite sport in summer?
items.note: A question about personal preferences. Favourite is the British spelling; American English favorite.

items.example: Which sports do you play with friends?
items.note: Use which to ask about a choice or selection of sports. Play typically combines with ball games.

items.pt: O de que mais gosto é ...
items.example: I like swimming best.
items.note: A preference pattern: I like + sport + best. In natural speech, replace the ellipsis with the sport.

items.example: I don't do any sports at the moment, but I enjoy watching matches.
items.note: Use any in a negative sentence. The book reinforces this negative response in exercise 23.3.

items.example: I'd like to do karate one day.
items.note: Would like + to + base verb expresses an activity someone wants to try. Replace the ellipsis with a sport.

items.example: My friends went skiing last winter.
items.note: Went is the irregular past tense of go; the sports collocation remains went skiing.

items.example: She does judo after school.
items.note: Does is the third-person singular present form of do, used here with judo.

items.example: We play badminton at the sports centre.
items.note: Badminton is a ball-game-group sport in this book; use play, not do or go.

items.example: They go snowboarding in the mountains.
items.note: The go + -ing rule in the teaching text applies to snowboarding.

items.example: Where do people play tennis in your town?
items.note: An exercise question answered with on a tennis court. Ask where to learn the place.

items.example: Some people prefer watching TV to playing sport.
items.note: Prefer is followed by -ing here. The exercise uses prefer watching TV as an alternative to sport.

learningObjectives: Identify and pronounce ball games, individual sports and martial arts illustrated in the source.
Choose play for ball games, go for -ing sporting activities, and do for judo and karate.
Name suitable playing locations and use on a court/pitch and in a swimming pool.
Ask and answer questions about the sports someone plays, does and enjoys most.
Discuss past participation, sports equipment and activities someone would like to try.

units.title: Unit 24 — Cinema
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 24. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.

items.example: We watched a western about cowboys.
items.note: A film set in the American West, often about cowboys.

items.example: The children enjoyed the cartoon.
items.note: An animated film or television programme; cartoon can also mean a humorous drawing.

items.example: I never watch horror films late at night.
items.note: A film intended to frighten people. Horror describes the type of film; frightened describes a person.

items.example: I watched a funny comedy yesterday.
items.note: A funny film or play intended to make people laugh. A comedy is a countable type of film.

items.example: This thriller has a surprising ending.
items.note: A suspenseful film with excitement, danger or mystery. A thriller need not be a horror film.

items.example: My friends enjoy action films.
items.note: A film with exciting physical events such as fights, chases or rescues.

items.example: She likes science fiction films about space.
items.note: A film involving imagined science or technology, space travel or other speculative ideas.

items.example: The musical has many songs.
items.note: A film or stage production that includes songs, and often dancing. It is also an adjective in other contexts.

items.example: We saw a romantic comedy together.
items.note: A film combining a love story with humour. Often abbreviated to rom-com in informal English.

items.example: What type of film do you like?
items.note: Type of + noun describes a category; in this unit it is a type or genre of film.

items.example: I like science fiction best.
items.note: A film and fiction genre. It can be used without the word film; the informal form is sci-fi.

items.pt: astro do cinema; estrela do cinema
items.example: That film star is very popular.
items.note: A famous actor known for performing in films. The plural is film stars.

items.example: My favourite actor is British.
items.note: A person who performs in films, plays or television programmes. This is a related teaching extension.

items.example: The director made three successful films.
items.note: A person who directs a film. The book gives the plural directors in section B.

items.example: She wants to be a film director.
items.note: A director working in cinema; a clarifying compound built from the source word directors.

items.pt: atuar em um filme; aparecer em um filme
items.example: My cousin was in a short film.
items.note: Be in a film means appear or act in it. Use in rather than on when referring to the film.

items.example: She played a famous character.
items.note: An actor plays a character in a film. The book illustrates this with an actor playing a named character.

items.example: He played an important role in the film.
items.note: Play a role means perform a character in a film or play. It is a useful extension of the source verb played.

items.example: I like films by that director.
items.note: Use by to identify who directed a film: films by a director. The book uses films by Italian directors.

items.example: Have you seen the new film?
items.note: Have you seen ...? asks about previous experience of watching something. Replace the ellipsis with a film title.

items.example: Did you like the film we saw?
items.note: Use did + the base form like when asking about a finished past experience. Not did you liked.

items.example: I loved it because it was funny.
items.note: A positive reaction to a film in the past. Loved is the past form of love.

items.example: I enjoyed it a lot.
items.note: A positive reaction to an experience. Enjoy takes a direct object: enjoyed it, not enjoyed of it.

items.example: The film was boring.
items.note: Boring describes something that causes boredom, such as a film. Bored describes how someone feels.

items.pt: O que está passando no cinema?
items.example: What's on at the cinema tonight?
items.note: A question about films currently showing at a cinema. Say on at the cinema, not on the cinema.

items.example: We go to the cinema on Fridays.
items.note: The standard British English phrase includes the article the: go to the cinema, not go to cinema.

items.example: We met at the cinema.
items.note: Use at to refer to the cinema as a place; in What’s on at the cinema?, on refers to films showing.

items.example: Let's watch a film at home.
items.note: Watch takes the film as a direct object, without a preposition. This is a useful related expression.

items.example: We saw a film last night.
items.note: See a film is a natural way to describe watching one. The past tense of see is saw.

items.example: We watched a DVD after dinner.
items.note: Say watch a DVD or watch DVDs. The source uses DVDs as a home-viewing option.

items.example: Do you go to the cinema often?
items.note: Often is an adverb of frequency. The book asks Do you go to the cinema often?

items.word: What is your favourite type of film?
items.pt: Qual é seu gênero de filme favorito?
items.ipa: /wɒt ɪz jɔː ˌfeɪvərɪt ˌtaɪp əv ˈfɪlm/
items.example: What is your favourite type of film?
items.note: Ask this to learn someone’s preferred genre. It is reinforced in the unit exercises.

items.pt: O gênero que mais gosto é ...
items.example: I like science fiction films best.
items.note: A common way to express the strongest preference. Replace the ellipsis with the film genre.

items.example: The film was on TV yesterday.
items.note: If a film is on TV, it is being shown or broadcast. This is a related use of the book’s on TV expression.

items.example: I prefer going to the cinema to watching TV.
items.note: Prefer + -ing can compare activities. With two activities, use prefer going ... to watching ... .

items.pt: descobrir o que está em cartaz
items.example: I checked online to find out what's on.
items.note: Find out means discover information. This expression refers to checking which films are showing.

items.example: Have you seen the latest film in the series?
items.note: Latest means most recent; the source uses latest when asking about a new film.

items.example: I saw that film on TV last weekend.
items.note: Use on TV for something shown on television, not in TV.

items.example: My grandparents still watch DVDs at home.
items.note: A source-era home-viewing expression. DVDs is the plural of DVD.

items.example: Who played the main character in that film?
items.note: The exercise asks who played a particular character; use the past tense played.

items.pt: astros do cinema; estrelas do cinema
items.example: Several famous film stars attended the event.
items.note: Plural of film star; the unit exercises reinforce stars as people in films.

learningObjectives: Identify the main types of films, including westerns, thrillers, horror films, musicals and romantic comedies.
Use film star, director, be in a film, play and films by to discuss film people and their work.
Ask whether someone has seen a film and give a natural opinion using loved, enjoyed and boring.
Use go to the cinema, on at the cinema, on TV and watch DVDs correctly.
Compare cinema and home viewing, describe preferences and ask which films are showing.
